clue.text: Firefighters will be damned

definitions.meaning: what firefighters will do is head off to fires, read literally
a dismissive curse telling someone to clear off to hell

explanation.walkthrough: The first reading takes the phrase literally: firefighters go to fires. The second is the old curse meaning 'go to hell', so 'be damned!'
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a mild oath equivalent to 'go to hell', and literally describes firefighters heading for fires.

clue.text: Look stupid, in spending a penny

indicators.note: in signals that the answer sits inside the run of words spending a penny

explanation.surface: Someone looks foolish while visiting the loo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spending a penny' is British slang for going to the toilet, but here it is just the text the answer hides in: spendinG A PEnny.
explanation.definitionFit: To stare open-mouthed is to look vacant or stupid, the sense of the verb here.

clue.text: An unappealing thing, by the way

definitions.meaning: something that puts you off or repels you
a side road leaving the main way, read literally

explanation.walkthrough: 'By the way' looks like the conversational aside, but it is a literal road junction: a branch off the road.
explanation.definitionFit: A noun for something off-putting, and also a junction where a road branches away from the main one.

clue.text: Pub files payment under "type which identifies the beast"

indicators.note: in a down clue, under places this piece below the one before it

parts.note: a brand is a type or make of goods

indicators.note: the pub files away, or holds, the payment, so it goes inside

parts.note: an inn is a pub
a giro is a payment by bank transfer, or a British benefit cheque

explanation.surface: A pub stores a payment beneath a notice about how livestock are marked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Files' looks like a noun; it is the verb, the pub storing the payment inside it. A giro was the old British state benefit payment, and 'under' works because this is a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A heated iron tool used to burn an owner's mark into the hide of cattle, so identifying each animal.

clue.text: Showing perfect circle

parts.note: A1 means first-rate or perfect, with the digit read as the letter I
a ring is a circle

explanation.surface: A display of a flawless ring.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 (first-class) is written with the numeral 1 doing duty as the letter I, a common crossword trick.
explanation.definitionFit: Giving something an airing is showing or broadcasting it, so the noun means a showing.

clue.text: Wind flower? See about that!

indicators.note: the see goes round about the flower, so one encloses the other

parts.note: Ely, a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire, is a bishop's see
an aster is a daisy-like flower

explanation.surface: A gardener points out a breezy bloom and invites a look.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' wants to be the definition, perhaps something flowing; 'Wind' is the definition. A see is a bishop's seat, and ELY is the crossword's favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: An easterly is a wind blowing from the east, a standard noun use.

clue.text: But you pro superstar?

parts.note: set against you, the speaker is I
con is the opposite of pro, as in pros and cons

explanation.surface: Someone protests that the other person supports the celebrity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'But' signals a contrast: if you are pro, then I am con, so each word gives its opposite, I and CON.
explanation.definitionFit: An icon is a revered celebrity, a superstar idolised by fans; the question mark admits the loose fit.

clue.text: Article in tribunal running on coat of arms

indicators.note: the article goes in the tribunal, inside it

parts.note: a court is a tribunal
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A tribunal hears a piece of writing about heraldry.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a heraldic term: a beast depicted courant is shown running.
explanation.definitionFit: In heraldry an animal shown at full speed is described by this French-derived word meaning running.

clue.text: The work of Tchaikovsky, eccentric, wonderful thing

parts.note: a nut is an eccentric person
a cracker is British slang for an excellent thing or person

explanation.surface: Someone praises a Tchaikovsky piece as odd but marvellous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cracker' for a wonderful thing is British informal usage ('a cracker of a goal').
explanation.definitionFit: Tchaikovsky wrote the famous Christmas ballet of this name.

clue.text: Hard layer finds way onto curly hairstyles

indicators.note: in an across clue, onto attaches the way after the hairstyles

parts.note: a perm is a curly hairstyle made with chemicals
an Afro is a bushy curly hairstyle
St is short for street, a way

explanation.surface: A stiff coating is found on curled hairdos.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural 'hairstyles' gives two: PERM and AFRO, then ST is added.
explanation.definitionFit: Permanently frozen ground forms a hard layer of subsoil in polar regions.

clue.text: To resign is not entirely pretty

indicators.note: not entirely means the word for pretty loses its final letter

parts.note: pretty means quite, as in pretty good

explanation.surface: Stepping down is described as somewhat attractive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pretty' looks like an adjective about looks, but it is the adverb meaning 'fairly', QUITE, which loses its E.
explanation.definitionFit: To quit a job is to resign from it, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Perhaps Washington capital for composer?

parts.note: Washington Irving was the American writer, so Washington is one example of an Irving
Berlin is the German capital

explanation.surface: Is the American capital the right name for a composer?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Washington' wants to be the US capital; it is the first name of the writer Washington Irving, so it points to IRVING.
explanation.definitionFit: The American songwriter of White Christmas, a celebrated composer of popular song.

clue.text: Winner of Olympics, behind, heard anthem of N Ireland?

parts.note: London won the bid to host the 2012 Olympic Games

indicators.note: heard signals that the word for behind is said aloud and spelt differently

parts.note: derriere is a genteel word for the behind or bottom

explanation.surface: A tune follows the Olympic host city's victory.
explanation.walkthrough: London won the 2012 Games bid shortly before this puzzle. The tune, also sung as Danny Boy, is an unofficial Northern Irish anthem, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: This traditional melody from County Londonderry serves as an unofficial anthem for Northern Ireland.

clue.text: Show young children where to go?

definitions.text: Show young children where to go?

parts.words: Show young children where to go?
parts.note: reads as giving directions to toddlers, but means teaching them to use the toilet

explanation.walkthrough: 'Where to go' sounds like directions; it is the toilet, and the verb means teaching toddlers to use one.
explanation.definitionFit: Toilet-training a toddler is literally showing the child where to go.

clue.text: Insult beyond the limit

parts.note: off means away from, beyond
an end is a limit or boundary

explanation.surface: An insult that goes too far.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beyond the limit' reads as one phrase meaning outrageous; it splits into two words, each with its own synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: To insult someone is to offend them; both verbs mean to give affront.

clue.text: One that's popped in name, returning circular? Not quite

indicators.note: returning means the combined letters are read backwards
the popped thing goes in the word for name

parts.note: to cite is to name or mention
a pill is something popped, swallowed as medicine

explanation.surface: A pill-popper cited as roundabout but not quite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returning' reverses everything built so far, not just the name. An ellipse is a squashed circle, so 'not quite' circular is fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Oval shapes are nearly round but flattened, so this adjective is close to circular without being it.

clue.text: May what's wrong blow it!

indicators.note: wrong signals that the letters of what are put in the wrong order

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written
a horn is something you blow

explanation.surface: An exasperated cry, as if wishing curses on something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'May' looks like the verb of a wish; it is the hawthorn's other name, from its blossoming in May.
explanation.definitionFit: May is the traditional name for hawthorn blossom, which flowers in that month.

clue.text: Where arrivals and departures are, confirming departure

definitions.meaning: a station or airport building handling arrivals and departures
describing an illness that makes death certain

explanation.walkthrough: 'Departure' in the second sense is death: a fatal illness is called this.
explanation.definitionFit: An airport building for travellers, and an adjective for a fatal disease that ends in death.

clue.text: Again suffer, consuming ecstasy for cure

indicators.note: the relived experience eats up the drug, so the letter goes inside

parts.note: to relive a hardship is to suffer it again
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: Someone suffers again after taking a drug as a remedy.
explanation.walkthrough: E for ecstasy is a standard crossword abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: To relieve pain is to ease or remedy it, close to curing.

clue.text: Torch that's delineating good egg

indicators.note: to delineate is to outline, so the letters for that's go round the rest

parts.note: i.e. stands for id est, that is
a nit is the egg of a louse

explanation.surface: A torch described as a lamp revealing a decent person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good egg' looks like a phrase for a decent person but splits into two pieces. 'Delineating' means outlining, so the abbreviation for that's wraps them.
explanation.definitionFit: To torch something is to set it alight, a verb sense matching ignite.

clue.text: Where you've got to be to win it, face not heading for first

parts.words: Where you've got to be to win it
parts.note: the slogan says you have to be in it to win it

indicators.note: not heading means the word for face loses its first letter

parts.note: dial is slang for the face

explanation.surface: A lottery-style slogan about competing, with a face losing out to first place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'You've got to be in it to win it' was the UK National Lottery slogan. DIAL is British slang for a face; dropping its head gives IAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Initial means first, as the initial stage is the first one.

clue.text: Good man enters mock, though his work's funny

indicators.note: the good man enters, going inside the word for mock

parts.note: to jeer is to mock
St, short for saint, is a good man

explanation.surface: A virtuous person joins in the mockery, though only as a comic.
explanation.walkthrough: ST (saint) is the crossword's usual good man. The definition describes the role: a court fool whose work is being funny.
explanation.definitionFit: A court fool was employed to entertain, so his job was being funny.

clue.text: Diabolical conversation? And here's its subject!

definitions.meaning: the remark made when the person just discussed walks in

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom is said when someone arrives just as they are being talked about; read literally it is conversation about the Devil.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom greets someone who turns up while being discussed, and literally means chatting about Satan.

clue.text: Free as this in prison?

definitions.meaning: doing ... is British slang for serving a prison sentence

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bird' for prison time comes from rhyming slang 'bird lime' for time; 'doing bird' means serving a sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: The simile 'free as a bird', and British slang for a prison term, as in doing bird.

clue.text: Top copy that's marked wrong

parts.note: to ape is to copy
a cross, X, is the mark for a wrong answer

explanation.surface: A best copy which the teacher has crossed out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top copy' reads as an original document; 'Top' is the definition and 'copy' gives APE.
explanation.definitionFit: The apex is the top or peak of something, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Italian artist's rejected starter accompanying wrong pasta

parts.note: a tort is a civil wrong in law

indicators.note: the artist's name has its first letter thrown out

parts.note: Bellini was a Venetian painter

explanation.surface: An Italian painter turns down an appetiser served with bad pasta.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starter' looks like a first course in this food scene; it is the first letter of BELLINI, which goes. 'Accompanying' simply puts the pieces side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Tortellini are small ring-shaped stuffed pasta, a specific kind of pasta.

clue.text: Non-voters?

parts.note: reads as people abstaining, but means those voting no in a division

explanation.walkthrough: 'Non-voters' looks like abstainers; read as 'No voters', it is those who vote against in Parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: In a parliamentary vote the votes against are counted as these, so they are no-voters.

clue.text: Smooth link under switches binding first of wires

indicators.note: the jumbled letters bind, or wrap round, the first of wires
switches means the letters of link under change places
first of means only the initial letter of wires is taken

explanation.surface: An electrical setup with a link beneath switches tied to the first wires.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Switches' looks like light switches in this wiring picture; it is the anagram signal. LINKUNDER rearranged to UNRINKLED wraps W.
explanation.definitionFit: Something without creases or wrinkles is smooth, as in an uncreased brow.
